name: Topical clindamycin

lead: Topical clindamycin is a prescription antibiotic gel, lotion or foam used for mild to moderate acne. People use it to cut down red, inflamed pimples and get a clearer complexion.

It reduces acne bacteria on the skin. It is usually combined with benzoyl peroxide or a retinoid, and reference sources report the combination works better than clindamycin alone. Randomised trials from the 1990s and 2000s compared clindamycin and benzoyl peroxide gels with each ingredient and with plain vehicle.

paras: It is applied to the affected skin as part of a prescribed routine, most often in a combination product with benzoyl peroxide. Pairing is intended to counter resistant bacteria. Improvement in inflamed lesions is typically judged over several weeks.

Dryness, burning, itching, peeling and contact dermatitis are reported in over 10% of users. Antibiotic resistance is a recognised concern, which is why it is rarely used alone. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Prescribed clindamycin gel or lotion reduces acne bacteria on the skin, so fewer inflamed pimples form and the complexion looks clearer. It is usually used with benzoyl peroxide and is well studied in clinical trials.

lead: Topical clindamycin is a prescription antibiotic lotion, gel or foam used for mild to moderate acne, often combined with benzoyl peroxide or a retinoid. It is a semisynthetic derivative of lincomycin, announced in 1966 and marketed since 1968 [1].

Wikipedia reports that adding benzoyl peroxide to clindamycin works better than clindamycin alone [1]. Randomised trials from the 1990s and 2000s compared clindamycin/benzoyl peroxide gels with each component and vehicle [2][3]. Topical use commonly causes dryness, burning or peeling in over 10% of users [1].
infobox: Cleocin, Dalacin; combinations BenzaClin, Duac, Acanya, Ziana

paras: Topical clindamycin phosphate treats mild to moderate acne. Combination products include clindamycin with benzoyl peroxide (BenzaClin, Duac, Acanya) and, in the US, clindamycin with tretinoin (Ziana) [1].

Topical effects include dryness, burning, itching, scaling and contact dermatitis [1]. Systemic clindamycin raises the risk of Clostridioides difficile colitis roughly fourfold in hospital settings [1]; that figure concerns systemic use.

Clindamycin binds the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit and inhibits protein synthesis [1]. Resistance is a recognised concern, and one trial rationale for combination products is suppressing resistant bacteria [3].

A pooled analysis of two double-blind trials compared clindamycin/benzoyl peroxide gel with each component and vehicle [2]. A 16-week randomised trial compared the combination with clindamycin alone for microbiologic activity and clinical efficacy [3][3]. A comparison of a foam and a gel formulation has been published [4], as have trials against nicotinamide gel [5][6] and a study of combination with adapalene [7]. Registered phase 3 trials include an adapalene-clindamycin gel (n=1617) [8] and clindamycin/benzoyl peroxide gels (n=1315, n=708) [9][10]. Detailed results are not summarised here.
